title: Hallucination Detection from Structural Reasoning Model
claim: Judging only outputs or whole linear traces misses unsupported steps; judging each step locally against its cited dependencies makes errors easier to find.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, red boxes mark each judge's visible context
description: Three side-by-side panels titled (a) Directly Judge, (b) Stepwise Judge, (c) Locally Judge, each flowing top to bottom from an Input ellipse to a light-green Output ellipse. In (a), a single arrow links Input to Output, and a red rounded box surrounds only the Input. In (b), a linear chain of three green squares, the last one hatched, sits between Input and Output. Many curved skip arrows run to later nodes, and a large red box encloses the Input and the first two steps. In (c), four grey condition squares fan out from Input into a DAG of green steps. A narrow red box covers only the two parent steps of a hatched judged step. A legend at the lower right defines Conditions, Steps, Judged steps and Judge text (red box). The eye goes first to the red boxes.
caption: Three views of using intermediate signals for hallucination scoring. (a) Judging only the final answer often leaves the verifier without enough supporting evidence. (b) Judging a full linear CoT exposes all prior steps, but when the trace is long, it is hard to pinpoint the relevant support for a step, so the judge can easily miss the key error. (c) Our approach first constructs a structural reasoning model (SRM) as a dependency DAG with explicit source citations, enabling local checks against the cited supports and making hallucinated or unsupported steps easier to detect.
abstract: Hallucinations pose a key challenge for large language models, and chain-of-thought prompting exposes intermediate reasoning but usually treats traces as linear sequences, making crossstep dependencies and unsupported intermediate claims difficult to identify. We propose a structural reasoning model to describe interactions among local reasoning steps. To detect hallucinations, we extract a directed acyclic reasoning graph over conditions and intermediate claims, verify each claim against its parent nodes, and aggregate the step signals with a simple mass-flow rule. Under a probabilistic erasure-gate abstraction, we interpret this aggregation as measuring information loss along the reasoning graph. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and HotpotQA show that the proposed method is most advantageous on longer, dependency-rich reasoning traces such as math and code generation, while remaining competitive on shorter factual QA; these results provide a structured perspective on chain-of-thought evaluation. All code and data are available at https://github.com/soncheinbok/FlowScore.
